en: Having first approached with devotion the All-pervading One, the Grandfather of all worlds, according to the Cārāyaṇīya Śikṣā,
I shall directly proclaim the Śikṣā; by that alone, the Grandfather is sufficient.
I shall proclaim the great science of phonetics (Mahāśikṣā) according to its sequence; listen to it, which is cherished by the wise, for the perpetual pacification of the impurities of speech.
[I shall also explain] the enumeration of the phonemes and their various designations and points of articulation.
The wise proclaim the ten locations of the letters—both vowels and consonants—in their entirety, from which the origin of all letters proceeds; hear them as I speak. 3–4.
The chest, the throat, the head, the palate, the teeth, the two lips, the nose,
the root of the tongue, the corners of the mouth, and likewise the roots of the teeth—
these, as well as the chest, the throat, and the head, are the three locations for the production of speech.
They say these are the *savana*s; in terms of their meaning, there is a distinction regarding the *sāva* and the *mātya*.

There are the acute (*udātta*), the guttural (*tālugarbha*), the circumflex (*svarita*), the protracted (*pracaya*), the grave (*nīca*), and the universal acute (*sārvānudātta*); likewise, there are the *sannatta* and the chest (*ura*).
One should pronounce a low vowel quickly, and one should draw out a high vowel as if from the back;
the teachers of phonetics know that the *svarita* occurs five times between the eyebrows. With the sixty-three consonants headed by the letter *ha*, [the vowels are combined].
The entire collection of speech is vast, immeasurable, and boundless. Those beginning with the letter *a* and ending with *au* are to be known as the fourteen vowels;
the remaining sounds are declared by those who contemplate syllables to be the consonants alone.
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are the twenty-five *sparśas* (stops).
Likewise, the letters from *ya* to *va* are the *antasthās* (semivowels), and *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the *ūṣmans* (sibilants and aspirate).
The articulation (*karaṇa*) of the *sparśas* is "contact" (*spṛṣṭa*), while that of the *antasthās* is otherwise.
They say that the *yama*s are closed (*saṃvṛta*), while the vowels and the sibilants (*svara* and *ūṣman*) are open (*vivṛta*).

The letters ending in the [four] classes are proclaimed to have four designations; the nasals (*nāsikya*) are nasalized (*ānunāsikya*), and the fifth letters of each class are designated as "final" (*antya*). 12–13.
The first and second letters of each varga, as well as śa, ṣa, and sa— these thirteen should be known as "unvoiced" (aghoṣa) by those who contemplate phonemes.
Furthermore, the production of unvoiced sounds is said to be like that of breath.

And it is certain that for all [consonants], the *nāda* is their unmanifested form (*akara*). However, for that which is emitted in a voiceless [consonant], there is the state of being the supreme locus. Furthermore, the *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, the *kalāpāṭha*, the *pluta*, and the *yamas* [are likewise].
The root of the tongue (jihvāmūla) and the labio-dental (upadhmāna)— these sixteen are dependent on others.
However, in the school of Ārāyaṇīya, there is always doubling (dvitva) of the anusvāra,
which has the resonance of a gourd-lute and follows the sounds of the dental root.

An *anusvāra* must always be applied after the sounds *h*, *r*, and *ḥ*, as well as before *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*. (17) A vowel with one *mātrā* is called short (*hrasva*), one with two *mātrās* is called long (*dīrgha*), and one with three *mātrās* is to be known as protracted (*pluta*); a consonant, however, has half a *mātrā*. (18)
The wise say that a short vowel joined with two mātrās is a *pluta* (protracted); a long vowel consists of three mātrās, while before a consonant it is half a mātrā.
One should employ short and protracted vowels at the pauses (*virāma*), but not nasalized ones.
However, for those beginning with the world of the gods (*svarloka*), there is no elision of the final consonants.
One should prescribe the vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) for all of them as consisting of two morae (*mātrā*), according to the illustrations in the treatises, for short, long, and protracted vowels.
If there were an end before and an end after, then that which stands in the middle would be of the same quality as the two preceding letters. However,
in a single word, a conjunct [consonant] is not [considered an "end"] until the fifth letter.
Yama should be understood as being like fire within a golden vessel; indeed, they are known thus.
The five vowels in pairs are short, while the remaining ones are long without exception.
Among those very same vowels, there are also protracted (pluta) forms, with the exception of the letters *ṛ* and *ḷ*.
The anusvāra is said to be "vidyādam" (based on the letter *m*); the jihvāmūlīya is based on *ka* and *kha*;
and that which is released as "iti" is called the upadhmānīya, which is based on *pha*.
Those phonemes which are bodiless (*aśarīra*) should be understood as dependent on others.
Resorting to another caste, they display their own true form.
Just as from the union of a husband and wife a child is born, so too from the union with another's support, a new caste and a new conjunction are produced.

Just as a person, being measured by previous words, is [defined] as auspicious, so too should the phonemes (varṇas) be understood as dependent on others; for they resort to that which is supreme—this is the second quarter-verse. 28.
There, in the center, stand the *yamās*, joined with the nasal (*nāsikya*) and the contact consonants (*sparśa*);
they are bodiless, divided into four types, and designated separately by their names.
The first [of these] is joined with the fifth [vowels], and there, in the center, is *kayam*. 29–30.
In the second [group] it is *khayama*, and in the third it is remembered as *gayama*.
Where they are seen in the fourth [group], conjoined with the final letters of the class (*varga*), there *ghayama* is to be known as situated in the middle, according to the Ārāyaṇīya school. 31.
The first *cayama* is known to be situated at the nose on the head;
the second should be assigned to the palate and the tongue,
and the third touches the ear, the teeth, and the ears.
The fourth [consonant] has its seat in the heart, and the nose; all the *yamas* are said to be gutturals (33).
There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate (34).
The gutturals are released from the throat; *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, and *ña* are said to be palatals;

*ṛ*, *ṭ*, *u*, *ra*, and *ṣa* are to be known as retroflex; *la*, *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, and *sa* are said to be dentals; *u*, *ū*, the upadhmānīya, and the labials (*pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma*) are labial; and *tu* and *ru* are released from the lips. (35)
The palatal and labio-palatal conjunct consonants are proclaimed to be guttural;
however, where the letter *ha* is seen followed by a soft vowel (*dak-svara*), they say that *ha* is guttural, but when it is with a consonant, it is from the chest (*aurasya*). 36–37.
The letter *a*, the *ka*-group (*kavarga*), and the *jihvāmūlīya*—

these nine letters are proclaimed to originate from the root of the tongue (38). Likewise, the *i*-vowel (*ivarṇa*), the *ca*-group (*cavarga*), and the letters *ya* and *śa* [originate from the palate].
These should be known as the subsequent consonants arising from the palate (tālu).
The letter *ḷ*, the *ta*-group (*tavarga*), and likewise the letters *la* and *sa*—these eight are to be known as dentals, arising from the roots of the teeth. 39–40.
The letter *u*, the labial class (*pavarga*), and the eighth letter [of the *ka*-class],
together with the *upadhmānīya*, are remembered as the ten labial sounds. If the letter *ha* is joined with a vowel, it is seen to be light.

One should know that [the letter] to be guttural; "hṛdaya" is the illustration. 42 The letter *ha* joined with the fifth [consonants] or even combined with the semivowels (*antastha*), one should know that to be chest-born (*urasya*); "āhriya" is the illustration. 43

Some wise scholars maintain that the *yama*s, the *anusvāra*, and the *nāsikya* arise from the very root [of the organs], while others hold that for the letter *a*, all places of articulation (*sthāna*) are involved; however,
for whichever specific phoneme no particular organ of production (*karaṇa*) is applicable, [it arises from the root].
In that context, the thesis is to be understood, for the grammatical treatise is of that very nature.
These sixty-three letters produced from the [six] places of articulation—by these alone the entire universe, the circle of speech, is pervaded. 45–46.
The vowels (sura) are said to be fourteen; the consonants (sparśas) are twenty-five;
the semi-vowels (yādayaḥ) are remembered as eight; and the sibilants (parāśrayāḥ) are sixteen.
These letters, numbering sixty-three, have been established by those who contemplate syllables.
The entire expanse of speech is pervaded by these alone, which have reached the further shore of the mudrās.

All the vowels are white in color; the letter *ī* resembles a consonant (*sparśa*); likewise, the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) and sibilants (*ūṣman*) are remembered as being dark blue, yellow, and red respectively. 48–49.
The *ayogavāha* consonants are dark-blue; all the vowels (*svara*) are remembered as white.
The semivowels (*antaḥstha*) are to be known as green, and the sibilants (*ūṣman*) have a reddish glow.
The stops (*sparśa*), when combined with the vowel *ī*, undoubtedly possess the colors of all the letters.

The *gaṇa* of the palatals (*tālavya*) beginning with *sa* belongs to Soma; those produced at the root of the tongue belong to Nirṛti. Those born from the throat belong to Agni, while the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) letters have Vāyu as their deity.
The dentals (*dantya*) are to be known as belonging to Rudra, and the labials (*auṣṭhya*) are considered to belong to the Aśvins.
The remaining [sounds] are undoubtedly to be known as belonging to the Vaiśvadevas;
thus the phonemes (varṇas) should be employed—neither indistinct nor distorted.
By the correct employment of the phonemes, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
By conquering this world through the *saṃhitā*, one would attain the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
This world is [the conquest] of the intermediate space; but by conquering the third world, heaven itself, one who has mastered the *krama* recitation is glorified in the world of Brahman.
Seated upon a mound of earth facing east, purified by purificatory rites and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Oṃ.
He should first employ the Praṇava, and immediately thereafter the Vyāhṛtis.
After reciting the Sāvitrī, one should then begin the narrative:
"Vasiṣṭha was performing austerities in the forest, a sage subsisting on roots and fruits; yet he who studies even a single Ṛg-verse attains that same merit as those [austerities]. (57–58)

The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability and the performance of the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes (mahāpātaka), swiftly. One should always perform one’s own duty as prescribed by the Veda without laziness.
For by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
Both the Vedic dharma and the dharma of action are the means for the ultimate liberation of the twice-born among sacrifices, austerities, and auspicious deeds.
Whatever fruit one enjoys by giving away the entire earth filled with all its riches,
that same fruit would belong to a twice-born man devoted to Vedic study who daily recites the Yajus formulas according to his ability, as if with ghee and nectar. (62)
They gratify the gods with clarified butter and likewise the ancestors with honey.
For him who studies his own Veda according to the rule, self-controlled and pure,
this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
Thus ends the first chapter, known as the *Cārāyaṇīya*.
Now, he states the definition of the phonemes that undergo euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*):
"As for those phonemes that have reached euphonic combination, their doubling is prescribed. (1)

One should indicate lightness through the absence [of a following consonant] and by means of a *sandhi*; that which is long, ending in a *visarjanīya*, at the end of a word, and joined with a *bindu*—
one hears the manifestation of such a conjunct (*saṃyoga*).
A single *anusvāra* dot is traditionally held to be released between two [consonants];

it is not seen as being like the *mūrdhanya* (retroflex) in the case of the *upaṅka* recitation. An *anusvāra* preceded by a short vowel should be understood to have a duration of one and a half *mātrās*.
The first [consonant] shall have half a mora; the reverse is the opposite case.

In the case of an *anusvāra*, however, there is always doubling according to the school of Ārāyaṇīya. Likewise, after a profligate woman has been threatened, and in the case of words such as *saṃskṛta* and others, [doubling occurs].
A celibate student and a wanton woman—that is how we two are refined [in speech].
In the case of the two *nara*s or the two *ha* sounds, a doubling occurs in certain instances;
however, this does not apply to the *jihvāmūlīya* or the *upadhmānīya*.

One should avoid the *sūrmī* (the "iron image") [sandhi] three times, and the *varṇavatī* (the "colored" sandhi) three times, according to the rule for the desired form of the syllables. Furthermore, there is no [sandhi] with semivowels (*antaḥstha*) joined with stops (*sparśa*),
nor with the second letters of a consonant class (*vargadvitīya*), nor ever with the fourth letters.
One should press the beginning, the end, and the middle with their own respective phonemes;
when one causes [the breath] to be smelled by the two Haras, the wise always cause it to transcend.
In the same way, one should indicate the jihvāmūlīya and the upadhmānīya.
After a vowel followed by *r*, there is a doubling of the following consonant.

However, after the letter *h*, [the doubling] occurs invariably even when it is not preceded by a vowel; for whenever there is a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) preceded by *r* or preceded by *h*, [the doubling takes place]. 10–11.
The supreme *dharma* of that [practice] is stated twice; it is the manifestation of Brahman wherein the two *ha*s are employed, and then the letter *ha* proceeds.
The unextracted is extracted, the resounding, and the lake is the illustration.
Where the letter *ha* stands in the middle between two *ra*s, one should know that this is the crossing of both; this is the illustration of fire (*agni*).
[The contact] of the letters *la*, *ra*, and *ha* is at the root of the tongue and the lips. 13–14.
But that which was previously mentioned as having two mātrās is remembered as "heavy" (guru);
it is my view that an anusvāra preceded by a short vowel has two mātrās. Those who contemplate phonemes (kṣara-cintaka) consider a short vowel followed by [a consonant] to have two mātrās.
One should always press the phonemes together like oil-seeds when they reach a junction;
however, those devoid of a junction should be treated like leaves.
A consonant following a vowel moves toward the next conjunction, provided another consonant follows.
Some [consonants] are prior, some are posterior, and some belong to both;
the conjunction is to be known as twofold: natural (*kṛta*) and artificial (*kṛtrima*).
That which arises in a single word is natural, while that which results from the junction of words is artificial.
In that regard, whether it be produced by a vowel or even if it is artificial, the preceding syllable of such [an element] shall be doubled— just as in *śśvoḥ*, *śścoḥ*, and *śśvam*. Furthermore,
the word ending in a consonant shall be the preceding [element], and the following [element] shall be its phoneme.

One should always recognize that doubling occurs at the time of a *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction) where two vowels are in immediate succession and designated as a *saṃyoga* (conjunction). In such a case, there shall be a double articulation; otherwise, there is a single articulation.
If there are two labial letters, provided they are not followed by a conjunct consonant,
one should perform the "double-labial" (*dviroṣṭita*) [pronunciation] for the sake of purifying the sight of the tongue.
It is desired that twenty-one letters undergo this doubling.

The first, last, and third [consonants], as well as *ya*, *la*, and *va*, together with *ṣa* and *sa*, and the semivowels (*antasthā*)—when these meet in conjunction (*sannipāta*), the wise one should first cause them to step across.
The *anusvāra* and the *visarga* are both bodiless (*aśarīrin*). 24.

Furthermore, in the *Ārāyaṇīyaka*, a doubling of these two [consonants] should be understood; however, the letters ś, ṣ, s, and h are never seen following a letter situated after them. Some say that there is a long vowel before a consonant cluster, while others maintain that it remains short.
If a closed sound (saṃvṛta) is seen following an anusvāra that lacks its own vowel,
it should be understood as a long anusvāra in the sacrifice;
these indeed are the supreme transitions among the phonemes, without a doubt.
In the conjunction of a semivowel (antasthā) and a stop (sparśa), the transition of the stop is observed.
But when there is a collision with a semivowel, the wise man should first apply the sequence, just as the waters indeed flow into the belly of a well. 28–29.
Where a conjunction of internal consonants (antastha), sibilants (ūṣman), or aspirates (paraspara) is observed,

one should declare that doubling of the contact-consonant (sparśa) in that instance, as in the words *kalmmāṣa* and *viśvavyacāḥ*. Likewise, where there are contacts joined on both sides with the sibilants *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*—
In that regard, this first sequence should be known by the wise, and no other; 31.

Where the *sparśa* consonants are joined with the fifth [nasal], and where the fifth [nasal] occurs at the end, there the designations of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) are seen, and in the middle of those, the *yamas* are situated. 32.
But when not the fifth [consonant] is joined with a single vowel, a *yama* is to be known at the fifth syllable, as in *rukkma*, *sa iḍḍhagnnigghghanti*,
and likewise *śaṣas*, provided that there is a nasal (*anunāsika*) following the conjunction.
One should recognize *yama* there in the view that "after each *snāta*, [a *yama* occurs]. In the fifth [section], which follows the four groups of four, there are *yamās*;
beginning with the letter *śa* and the letter *cha*, it is designated as the triad of *saṃnata*. 34–35.
Where consonants (*sparśa*) are not seen joined with the final letters of their respective classes (*vargānta*), there the semi-vowels (*yama*) cease, just as kinsmen depart from a cremation ground.
[A consonant] joined with the final letter of its class, with the sibilants (*ūṣman*), or even with an internal nasal (*antaḥstha*), [is subject to the same rule]. 36.
Having seen [the signs], they abide by the restraints like a traveler following an instruction.
(37) When the final consonants of both [words] are joined together, like a man wearing earrings, one should know that it is *ayasantam*; "saṃjñāna" is the illustration for this. (38)
In the *saṃjñātana* [section], the penultimate vowel is long, and one should not prescribe an *anusvāra*. Having joined it with the letter *ña*, one proceeds; *ṅa* and *ña* are light.
Likewise, the penultimate vowel is nasalized (*anunāsika*), as are the *anusvāra* and the letter *e*.
One should avoid crying out or making indistinct sounds when pronouncing *saṃjñāna*.
A wise person should pronounce the vowels with equal and smooth continuity, without breaking the flow;
it is not possible for those untrained in grammar to speak correctly.

Where the letter *ha* is joined with the fifth [consonants of the five classes] according to the rule, a nasal sound (*nāsikya*) is inserted between those two, just as a Brāhmaṇa is placed between the *pa* and *ha* sounds in the word *pahṇu*. One should not emit the breath through the nostrils during the conjunction of *ha* and *sa*.
One should not pronounce the sound with the chest up to the navel, nor likewise among the Hayanava [Vedic] schools.
If the letter *ha* is seen to be light when joined with a vowel, one should know it as guttural; "with the heart" (*hṛdaya*) is the illustration for this.
If it is seen to possess the consonant *ha* in its state of heaviness (*gurutva*), one should know that to be *uraḥstha*; "āhriya" is the illustrative example (45).
Furthermore, among the nasalized (*nāsikya*) phonemes, whichever vowel is employed in a particular place [is the *sthāna*].
They subsist on each of those very [sounds], and one should avoid the defects of the nose (nasādoṣa). 46.

In the case of doubt between the vowel *ṛ* and the letter *r*, one should know that the preceding consonant carries the weight (*bhārika*) of the *r*; however, when it occurs before the vowel *ṛ*, it becomes light (*laghu*). 47.

The letters *ṅ*, *ṇ*, *n*, and *ṃ* should be separated by the intervention of *ka*, *ṭ*, or *ta* when followed by *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*; one should avoid [their coalescence], as they are joined together. The first sibilant (*ś*), when joined with another sibilant, occurs either within a word or at the beginning of a word.
One should not recognize this [sound] as being like the fish in the water or the *opasara* [insects];
likewise, when the letters *ṭa* and *śa* are joined with *pa*, it should be so for *ka* and *śa*.
One should show their own form, but the second [consonant] should be elided. 49–50.
The six syllables of the *ṣaṭpātra* mantra are *vi-ri-pū-śi-n-u*, which is the rising [mantra];
and likewise, where there is the word *anukṣāti*, there one should emit the second [syllable] into the form of the monkey (*kapin*).
51. In that [form], one should release the second [syllable] into the monkey's own nature.
Elsewhere, when the first [foot] is of such a kind as to consist of one quarter joined with *uṣman* (sibilants),
and having recognized that in the second [foot], it is declared to be an *anuṣṭubh* with *śāra*.
The third and the fourth [feet] are words following the fourth and so forth.
In the *triṣuggharma* [section], the modification is not applied; however, it is traditionally taught that when the letter *ña* follows *kakāra*, there is the substitution of *cha* for *śakāra*.
Furthermore, this applies to the substitution of *cha* for *śakāra* and other similar cases as well. 54.
But when released before a voiceless [consonant], there is the substitution of the following position;
this applies always in the case of *kṣa* and so forth, as well as when followed by another [consonant] that remains in its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
One should not apply [the rule] to those beginning with *saṃskṛta*, nor likewise to what precedes or follows them.

At the beginning of a *ṛc*, a half-verse (*ardharca*), or a section (*anuvāka*), as well as when there is a break in the accent, a *puṃścalī* (breath-pause) should likewise occur; and the *uṣman* [sibilant] remains in its place before another *uṣman*.
This rule regarding the sequence of phonemes is the opinion of Ārāyaṇi.
The locus of vowels for all systems of phonetics is now declared:
a letter does not proceed [in its proper order] unless it possesses a vowel, even if it has been acquired many times through various causes.
Chapter Two.
And this non-composition [of the phonemes] shall now be explained, for it is concise;
in some cases there is a sandhi with a consonant, and likewise in some cases with a vowel.
Thus says Sanatkumāra:
The teachers who contemplate sound say that a syllable (*akṣara*) is a vowel; for them, a word (*pada*) is a collection of these [syllables], and it is established as being fourfold:
that which is nasal (*nāsikya*), that which is called *abhika*, both, and that which is immediately following a prefix (*naipātika*).

An *upasarga* (preverb), a noun (*niṣpatti*), and a verb (*pada*)—thus the word is fourfold. "Nāsikam," "savitā," and "vyoma" are examples of nouns; "vy-ṛtu" is recorded as an example of a verb. "Pari," "upa," and "ati" are *upasargas*, while "ca" and "vā" are cited as examples [of particles].
It is not desired that it be declared as belonging to the Asuras, Vāyu, Indra, or Soma;
rather, its prefix is said to be Āgneya and its suffix is remembered as Vāruṇa.
It is declared to be Bhāradvājaka by name and Bhārgava by lineage.

The *upasargas* are remembered as belonging to Vasiṣṭha, while the *nipātas* are remembered as belonging to Kāśyapa. Elision (*lopa*) and euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) belong to Soma; *tyāga* is remembered as belonging to Candra.
*Vajyasi* is a modification (*vikāra*), while *prakṛti* belongs to Kiṃsvid. (6–7)
The non-perception of a phoneme is elision (*lopa*); the perception of a phoneme is augmentation (*āgama*).
Change of phoneme is modification (*vikāra*), while its inherent nature is known as the original form (*prakṛti*).
Augmentation of a phoneme, transposition of a phoneme, as well as two others—modification and destruction of a phoneme—are [the six types of change].
Likewise, *niyoga* is the excellence of meaning; that is called the fivefold etymology (*nirukta*).
Short *saṃdhi*, as well as long [vowel], with a vowel and with a consonant—thus it is fourfold. I shall explain *saṃdhi* accordingly: "Agni indeed was in front, not consciousness" (RV 10.8.2). 10.
Two [consonants] are long, or short and long; long and short are adjacent, or even when both are short, one is long in summary.
It revolves to the right.

This is the rule of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*): when a word ending in *a* is followed by a word beginning with *i*, and likewise when it is followed by a word beginning with *u*, both vowels become joined with the letter *r*. When a vowel beginning with *ṛ* follows a word ending in *a*, that vowel becomes *r*.
It should be joined with the following [consonant], as in the example "yathartu.
For wherever there is that supreme state beginning with the vowel *ṛ* and ending with the vowel *a*, in each such instance, the letter *ra* shall be joined with the following [consonant]. 13–14.

The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of clarity: in the case of *saṃdhi*-vowels, when following a word ending in the vowel *a*, the first of the second class [consonants] becomes the second, and the first of the third class becomes the fourth; such is their transformation. (15) Because of the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, a deviation from this rule is observed in certain instances.
"apānte sarśādayāmi," and so forth.
(16) When a word ending in *i* is followed by a word beginning with a vowel in a compound, one should perform the sandhi; however, if the preceding word ends in *u*, the rule is optional. (17)

Varuṇa is directly perceived as stationary; in brief, there is a hiatus (*vivṛtti*) from a conjunct consonant (*saṃdhi-varṇa*) when followed by a vowel, except for those preceded by a short vowel. Furthermore, there is no hiatus after a word ending in *a*, *i*, or *u* when followed by a word beginning with a long vowel. 18. After a word ending in *e* or *o*, there is no hiatus before a word beginning with *a*.
Some desire a single sandhi, while others [desire] a *vivṛtti*-sandhi.

Just as there is a sandhi in odd-numbered [syllables] when an *a*-final is followed by a vowel, they say that the same sandhi occurs in even-numbered [syllables], and a long vowel follows immediately thereafter. 19–20.

Regarding that which is twice-produced from the throat, some authorities say it becomes both [voiced and unvoiced] when followed by a voiced sound, while others say there is elision when followed by a sound other than that; likewise, after a long vowel, there is a doubling when a vowel follows.
For this twice-produced [consonant], there is no loss of its syllabic nature when preceded by a voiced sound, nor does it take on the quality of *repha* (the *r*-sound).

They say that there is elision (*lopam*) before the letter *ra*; however, when the vowels *i* and *u* are followed by *ra*, they become long. When the letter *ra* follows the vowels *i* and *u*, at the time of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), those two vowels become long; otherwise, it is a case of *repha-saṃdhi*.

The letter *ra* is the first [consonant] of the throat; furthermore, the remaining letters ending in *a* and so forth are, in brief, [the first] in relation to the following voiced sounds. Otherwise, for the palatal, retroflex, and dental classes, the first two letters of each class [are the first]. (24)

And where a single consonant at the beginning is released and joined with a sibilant (ūṣman), it becomes the fifth of its own class; when a first [consonant] is followed by a fifth, it becomes the third; and when followed by a voiced sound (ghoṣa), the first and so forth attain their own nature.

Before a following *sparśa* (stop), a final *m* becomes *anusvāra*; before a following semivowel (*antastha*) or sibilant (*ūṣman*), it becomes the nasal of its own class (*savarṇa*). In the case of *yajñeṣu*, *kataḥ*, *utvoṃ*, and *viṣṭaḥ*, [the rules apply]. 27.
*yajñeṣu kata utvoṃyya viṣṭaḥ*.

When an anusvāra follows and a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga) stands before it, one should recognize that [the preceding vowel] as short; this is the illustration for "having established. Furthermore, in some cases, the closed (saṃvṛta) [vowel] is seen following an anusvāra. 28–29.

One should understand that even when long, [the vowels] beginning with *i* and *u* are subject to elision (*lopa*) upon hearing the sacrificial formula (*yajña*), provided they have a short vowel as their penultimate (*upadhā*).

However, in words beginning with a vowel, the nasalized sounds (*draṇanāḥ*) remain. Sitting facing west, one should recognize them as heavy (*guru*) everywhere, as well as those preceded by a short or long vowel.

In the sequence of vehicles and conveyances, however, within the constituent parts of a compound, a consonant [is doubled] when followed by an *ṛ*-vowel; it is always doubled before a conjunct, with the exception of the letter *r*. A word ending in a consonant—such as *nṛ*, *su*, *yat*, or *an*—is the preceding element, while the following consonant is the subsequent syllable. 31–32.

When joined with an *ṛ*-vowel, that [consonant] becomes heavy by virtue of that combination. They pronounce the desired *k* and *d* clusters from the first sibilant (*ṣ*), provided it has become the second [sibilant] in the following word.
Furthermore, the first [consonant] is joined in the middle, as is the nasal sibilant (*ṇ*) with the [following] sibilant.
The junction of the hundred colors at the rising of that Sāvitra [sun] ends in the letter *na*; 34.

As if created twice, it possesses the letter *ra* after the letter *ma*, and when followed by other letters beginning with *ra*, it becomes an *anusvāra*; however, in the two words *saṃgasam* and *sarvam*, the *repha* remains. 35.
If there is no *rāṭ* (the letter *r*) following [the first word], the *anusvāra* is not prescribed between those two;

in the compound *samrāṭ*, [the *anusvāra*] occurs after the palatal *t* (*tālvya*) that follows the *t*. The letter *cch* together with *y*, and the letter *l*, are indeed equal [in their application]. 36.
That which is the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is a peaceful couple from the heavenly world.

(37) Having first performed the word-division (*padaccheda*), one should thereafter perform the compound (*samāsa*); once the compound has been formed, the wise man should subsequently explain its meaning. (38)
The rule for the *saṃhitā* has been proclaimed out of compassion for poets;
it was formerly practiced repeatedly by the wise, just as Keśava [was followed] by his soldiers.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Cārāyaṇī Śikṣā.

A mantra that is deficient in accent (*svara*) or phoneme (*varṇa*), or is incorrectly employed, does not convey its own meaning; like the Vajra of Speech, it destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [Pralhāda] was destroyed due to an error in accent.
One who has consumed food obtained from an improper place, or eaten at an improper time, is destroyed.
There is no liberation for him from evil, as if from a venomous snake, for those who are difficult to subdue.
But that which has come from a good source, is well-chewed, properly recited,
well-established, melodious, and well-articulated— such Vedic speech shines like a king.

Just as a tigress carries her cub with her teeth, neither biting him nor letting him fall through fear of injuring him, so should one employ the phonemes. The speech should be sweet yet not indistinct, and distinct yet not harsh.
In this land of Sanātha, nine types of vocal qualities have come into being: sweetness, clarity of syllables, proper division of words, as well as speed, steadiness,
and the balance of heavy and light syllables— these six are the virtues of recitation.
One should know that the first *savana* is like the roar of a tiger, constant and situated in the chest;
the midday [savana] is like the cooing of a cakravāka bird, situated in the throat.
One should know the third *savana* to be human.
That [Veda] located in the head should always be employed;
a wise man should never recite the Veda as composed by them [the poets], treating speech as independent,
but rather with even-paced, well-restrained, neither too fast nor too slow [intonation].
One should utter auspicious speech that conforms to the sacred scriptures.
(10) If one utters the *tāra* vowel in the forenoon of the ninth day, his enthusiasm perishes during the night, just as it does through sexual intercourse. (11)
One should recite the Moon of Liberation, encircled by gentleness;
the recitation should resemble ten million moons, enriched with vowels, in a moderate tone.
One should transition from vowel to vowel, joining the vowels without harshness.
One should make the cut even, fine, with shade, heat, and essence (13).
One should always recite with an even tone and demonstrate the path with the hand;
whatever place the voice reaches, that one should demonstrate with the hand (14).
As is the voice, so is the hand; one should avoid discordant sounds.
Wherever the voice and the hand are situated, there they go together, just as the hands of men follow their tone, whether auspicious or inauspicious. 15.
The gaze follows the hand, or it moves in accordance with the shadow.

Having made speech follow the hand, and having made the gaze follow the mind, one brings the gaze under the control of the hand; such is the characteristic of the threefold modulation of voice (*traisvarya*). 16–17.
In terms of pitch, a low tone is called *svara* (vowel), while [the high-pitched] is called *svarita*.
Those who contemplate the phonemes say that in the threefold intonation (*traisvarya*), the accent (*svara*) is the primary element.
Seated comfortably for a long time with a one-pointed mind, he should remain free from fear and the reliance on pride.

One who eats and drinks according to the season and with proper moderation should recite the Veda, avoiding defects in pronunciation. By casting a glance with the right eye, one should diminish the intensity of the vision; the wise know that the junction of the nose, cheek, and eyebrow is the domain for the *udātta* accent.

The *puṭi*, the *sphuṭi*, the *vīṇā*, the *muṣṭika* shaped like a bow—these six are defects of the hand; the *paraśu* is the seventh. [The hand] should be turned upward (*uttāna*), slightly elevated, with the fingers clearly defined and adorned.
One should produce the pierced vowel (svara-viddha) as reaching toward the forefinger (prādeśa).
The acute (udātta) is produced from the interior of the palate (tālugarbha), and that which follows it is likewise from the interior of the palate;
however, in the case of a combination (samāhāra), it is the circumflex (svarita), while the protracted (pracaya) follows behind it.
The low-pitched (nīca) syllable is lower than the unraised (anutta), and the one ascending from there is still lower; these seven are the highest among all the udātta and anudātta tones.
A word-final syllable may sometimes be udātta, or it may be udātta [in other positions].
The following word shall be udātta; that is called tālugarbha.
Whatever syllable occurs immediately after a svarita, the wise declare that one should recognize as pracaya. 25–26.
They say that for the sake of clarity, all vowels should be pronounced with an udātta accent; however, those that are low should be uttered very low.
If that [following vowel] is also low, the wise call it *sannatara*. 27.
One should know that the *svarita* accent extends for one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), where the supreme state is high;
even if the word is low, it should become *svarita* over the span of one finger-breadth.
(28) O Agni, O Sovereign, O One-footed, O Āhavanīya!
Or he sacrifices on the new moon day with the hymn "kayā śubhā" (RV 4.31.1).
Furthermore, in the Ārāyaṇīyaka, it should be understood that the tongue touches the palate and the chin, yet neither the voice nor the hand [reaches] there. 29–30.
In the Cārāyaṇīya Śikṣā, the fourth chapter:
"The vowels are said to be of eight kinds; I shall describe them in their proper order.
One should know that there are four oblique [vowels] and four straight ones."
A syllable that contains the sound *sa*, or even one that is unaccented (*an-udātta*) yet followed by a circumflex (*svarita*) word—
whether preceded by a low-pitched vowel (*nīca*) or not— is called the *jātya* accent. It is thus established.

And in the *ājya* [verse], where the vowel *a* is seen following two acute (*udātta*) vowels and is itself unaccented (*anudātta*), there is the *abhinihita* sandhi; for example, "tasmai vājam" (RV 10.128.4).
Thus, "so 'haṃ vājasaniḥ" becomes "so 'haṃ vājasaniḥ," and "tasmai vājaṃ sūvāntam."

If the vowels *i* and *u* become *y* and *v* respectively when followed by a high-pitched (*udātta*) vowel, and [the preceding vowel] is always low-pitched (*nīca*) before a following suffix, one should know that this is the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* [svarita]. For example:
*asvakaṃ*, *yajāmahe*, *dvyannaḥ*, *sarpiḥ*.
Where there is elision of the vowel *i*, it is joined with the vowel *i* itself;
both the acute (*udātta*) and the grave (*anudātta*) [vowels] are thus fused, as in "abhīndhatām.
The short vowel *i* is the original form for both the high-pitched (*ī*) and low-pitched (*i*) vowels.
When a vowel is pronounced as a continuous glide, it is likewise perceived as circumflex (*svarita*). Whatever word in the Veda has an acute (*udātta*) vowel preceding it and is itself circumflex,
this is called the *tairovyañjana*, which possesses the greatest variety of accents.

One should know that [the vowel] following an avagraha is to be pronounced with the *īḍā* (circumflex) accent when there is a svarita immediately after it; however, if the avagraha itself is udātta, then one should recognize a pause (*virāma*) after it. 9.
Where there are high and low tones in the word *gopatau*, if the pause (*avagraha*) occurs on the low tone, one should understand that it must be treated as such; thus say the wise. 10.
Just as when a bow is drawn and released at the head, the string returns again to its own place, so too, when the vowel has disappeared,
that which belongs to the *praśliṣṭa*, *kṣaipra*, and *jāti* [svarita] accents shall likewise occur here.

The *udātta* (high-pitched) accent occurring among those [vowels] is proclaimed to belong to one part [of the syllable]. It never belongs to the preceding part (*pūrvāṅga*) nor to the subsequent part (*aparāṅga*) when accompanied by a *svarita*.
When both are joined together, the wise man should make the opening (*dvāra*). 12–13.
The word with the acute accent on the final syllable should be placed first, or in some cases it may be acute on the first;
he does not cast his hand down low wherever he goes—may your fortune never abandon him. 14.

Regarding the *patnī* [note] following an unaccented [syllable], where there is a tremor of two finger-breadths, the wise practitioner should cause the hand, moving along the back [of the palm], to vibrate while joined with the *svara* [pitch]. 15
O gods, where there is a trembling of another's meaning from a svarita accent, the finger should be raised above [the head];
when the hand has reached the ear and trembles, one should extend it beyond three fingers' breadth. 16.

The vigorous, unanointed [fingers] move downward; having descended, the raised finger likewise moves toward it, and then one should perform a tremor. After that, the hand goes back to that very place. [This is] the *saṃvāvasa* of Agni.

Whenever both knees are at one place together, the second [knee] should be one and a half finger-breadths above the first; this is the human posture (mānuṣāsana). 18. From this, [the other postures arise].
The *sādhā* [tune] is said to arise from the trembling of the fingers in all positions;
some who know the notes maintain that these are proclaimed as varieties of *māyā*.
Chapter Five.
Just as the lord of the Saumantana Nagas runs from step to step,
so too each step should be clearly visible and distinct;
however, when there is a pause at the end of a step, it is known as the *balāhaka* [caesura].
That which pauses at the end of half-verses is called Vaidyuta; that which pauses at the end of a quarter-verse is Bhujaṅgama;
that which pauses at every word is called Viśikha;
and when it pauses in other meters, the wise know that as Parvaka.
The *pratiga* has a slender middle; its foot consists of six syllables.
The *kumāralalita* has seven, while the *anuṣṭubh* has eight syllables.
The *phalayuta* has nine, and the *praṇava* has ten syllables.
The eleventh is Upendravajrā, while the twelfth is Jaloddhṛta;
the metrical foot of thirteen syllables is called the Praharṣa metre (5).
They know the metre of fourteen syllables to be Vasantatilakā.
The fifteenth is Mālinī, while they know Ṛṣabha to be the sixteenth;
Mandākrāntā always has seventeen syllables per foot,
Sugītakarṇa has eighteen, and Śārdūla has nineteen.
The *suvadanā* has twenty syllables, the *sragdharā* has twenty-one,
the *abhravṛtta* has twenty-two, and the *sulalitā* has twenty-three. Next is the *krauñcapāda*, which consists of twenty-four syllables.
The twenty-eighth foot is *śobhana*, and the twenty-ninth is *bhujaṅga*;
the twenty-sixth is *madhukara*, and after that comes *para*.
In this *yoni*, there are thirty feet; understand this as the *āryā* meter. 10.
Otherwise, it would be prose (*gadya*).

Where there is a metrical foot (*pāda*), and where a word consisting of gutturals, dentals, or the last eight [consonants] occurs, and likewise the following word begins with a similar sound, the wise know that as *virāma*.

The vowel that is placed upon the surface [of the alphabet] by the mere closing of the eyes of one whose sight is swift is called *dīrgha* (long) from its double occurrence, and *pluta* (protracted) from its triple occurrence. 12.

One should know the maṇḍala to be situated in the heart; one should know the *dvirāṇava* (two-atom) in the throat. The *trirāṇava* (three-atom), however, is the *mātṛka* (alphabet) spread upon the tip of the tongue.
A blue jay utters a measure (*mātrā*) of two measures, which would be the age [of the sound]. 13–14.
The crest [of the flame] is to be known as having three measures; this is the grasping of the measure.
Like lightning situated in the sky, or like a thread through a gem, or like the cutting of fibers in the case of strength—such is the severing of the revolutions. 15.
The interval between four *vivṛtti*s shall be a *mātṛkā*. For others it is half a *mātrā*, and for others it is a full *mātrā*.
Where both [the preceding and following] are long, the intervening space is a *mātṛkā*. 16–17.

The *yava* and *āyava* measures were first established at the beginning; half of that [is the measure] for the two short vowels, and half again for the short vowel and so forth; likewise, the *vatsānusṛtā* and *vatsānuvāriṇī* are at the beginning. 18.
The *Pāvakavatī* [has] short vowels at both ends and long vowels in the middle; this is the *Pipīlikā* [meter].
This is the sixth chapter of the *Cārāyaṇī-Śikṣā*.
Padracitā, Avalagātārā, Keśinī, Dhātrī, Svamatipipīlikā, Anvaṣṭrā, Vāyavyā, and Avaṣṛtti— these are the eight [goddesses].
Of these, three, three, and three [groups] are respectively located in the east, the middle, and the north.
At the ritual recitations (*savanas*), the fast, medium, and slow tempos are praised.
For the purpose of practice, one should employ the fast tempo; for the purpose of performance, the medium;
and for the purpose of instruction to students, one should employ the slow tempo.
The wise declare that recitation which is joined according to the sequence of words, established by the rules of phonetics (*yajñadharma*),

and characterized by the proper union of place of articulation, hand-gesture, and tone, is "fast" (*druta*). Furthermore, when there is a junction of a light syllable and so forth with a heavy one, and it is closely followed by its own breath-group at every step, it is likewise [so described].

One should make the duration of the morae equal; that is declared to be the medium [tempo]. When each word and each step are distinct, and the movement is joined with the measure of the breath, that mode of application in the placement [of the syllables] is the slow tempo.
The instrumental music of the *tāṇḍava* and other dances follows the sequence for the sake of the measure (*mātrā*), even while transcending it, for the purpose of the disciple's practice.
When the Guru, being angry, utters words toward the disciple at night that are like the forest fire or the sun—
Those empty, well-practiced words burn [only for a moment], but afterwards they become like white lotuses cooled by the rays of the moon.
(8) Thus ends the seventh chapter.
The first letters of the *da*-group and the fifth letters [of each group] are to be consumed, and indeed, the fifth letters are to be consumed.
Among those situated within, two *lava*s have eaten; the rest remain hungry.
In each group (*varga*), the first two should be given ten syllables (*varṇa*);
by joining them with others, the practice of feeding is praised.

One should avoid the *ya*, *kta*, *ha*, *li*, *kṣṇa*, *patnī*, and *vān* sounds when they touch one another; however, having excluded the fifth [consonant] from each group, one should diligently consume that which contains the *ṅa* sound among the fifth consonants. 3.
He places the gold plate; he does not place it with the word "vāc" (speech).

There are five at the end, three semivowels (*antasthā*), and some say two *la*s in the *pada*. Up to the final [syllable], there are four final syllables to be consumed, consisting of fifteen syllables.

The sacrifice of the forest consists of eight syllables beginning with *ya* and ending with *ha*; these four groups of four, when combined, form the sixteen-syllable mantra that is both offered and consumed. 5.
The wind blows in all directions;
the third and fifth [notes] are to be excluded, while the remaining members of the group are not to be consumed.
With a single step, the nasal sounds [are reached]; this is the honey for one who has been initiated.
In the *udgātṛ* [chant], one should avoid those that are mutually touched; the third [class of consonants] is accepted from the fifth [vowel].
The semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) joined with [the nasals] are like wine, and are not to be consumed by the twice-born.
O Agni, among these seven [groups], the second and third consist of even and odd [vowels] respectively; the fourth consists of semivowels (antaḥstha) joined with sibilants (ūṣman).
As for the fifth, which is the junction (sandhi), I shall explain it here according to my understanding.
They know that the vowels *i* and *e* have arrived at the tongue and palate;
however, in the Cārāyaṇīyaka school, there is the consumption of the *piṇḍas* of the *saṃpreṣyas*.
The letter *ya* is joined to the two *ha*s clearly, and not anywhere else.

In the letter *ha*, there is clearly the beginning; in the letter *kā*, the *repha*; and in the vowel *ṛ*, that indeed is Agni. Among men, he is their vigor (*vīrya*), and he is that very [vigor] itself.
He is indeed Agni; among men, he is their unassailable vigor.

From the mass of flames, he fashioned the nasal organs together with their anusvāras from clay; likewise, he formed the secondary vowels and the masses of air, and for the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), the roots of the tongue;
and for Brahmā, the organ of speech.

One should describe the restraint (*saṃyama*) as being like a mass of cotton wool situated within other things, such as wood; it is devoid of internal movement. When the state of being is divided into its constituent parts, the person becomes a mere fragment.
When there is confusion regarding the dental and palatal [pronunciations] in a single word— such as when a person pronounces the letter *cha* with its proper duration as palatal,
while others say it is dental in the case of the letter *sa*— this is a lapse of memory due to their lack of distinction. (15–16)
*Gachagachakalaścaiva*, *yachataśca yoreva ca*, *icha ṛcha tathā aicha*— people find these palatal sounds [in the Veda].
(17) *Pravatsyan yasutovatsaḥ*, *nihotāsatsipitsaru*.
"May you release again, may you place [it] again; what was released again shall remain.
Desiring to rise up, desiring to give, I shall restrain you with that which is not to be given.
You who were about to perish, you shall not perish; O performer of the rite, may you two physicians heal."
The year shall hunger; the Maruts indeed desire to eat us up.
They shall not let us rise; they shall devour us. O Kutsas, you shall know this right here.
From the rising place, the *abhitsāra* (assailant) strikes; Varuṇa strikes with his missile.

One should know that [the letter] joined with *utsa*, *yatotsa*, or those uttered separately at the end, as well as *ha* joined with the fifth [consonants] or with the semivowels (*antastha*), is guttural (*aurasya*); they say that when uncombined, it is guttural (*kaṇṭhya*). 21–22.

One should not release breath through the nostrils during the conjunction of the *ha* and *sa* sounds; nor should one emit a loud sound from the chest while eating excessively, nor likewise when in forests.
Brahmā is the lord of the gods; may speech protect him.
Wherever a vowel is seen following the letter *ha*, that *ha* is known to be guttural (*kaṇṭhya*). However, when it is followed by a consonant, it is guttural (*kaṇṭhya*) or chest-born (*aurasya*).
One should understand that which is preceded by [a guttural] and ends with a chest-born [consonant] as being "chest-born" (*urasyanta*); this is the illustrative example. 24–25.

If the letter *ha* is seen joined with a vowel and possesses lightness (*laghutva*), one should know it to be guttural (*kaṇṭhya*); this is the illustration regarding the heart (*hṛdaya*). (26) Furthermore, the letter *ha*, as the fifth [consonant], when joined with the heart or even conjoined with the *mantras* of the breaths, resides in the chest (*kakṣya*).
Between those two, that which is called *nāsikya* is said to belong to Brahmā.
The *svarabhakti* (vowel-fragment) is to be known as twofold: occurring before the letter *l* and before the letter *r*.
It is further classified by those who contemplate the nature of syllables as being either vowel-accented (*udātta*) or consonant-accented (*anudātta*).

One should know *kariṇī* when there are the letters *ra* and *ha*; *karviṇī* when there are *ra* and *śa*; one should know *hariṇī* when there are *la* and *śa*; and *trīturā* when there are *dhāṃ* and the letters *tu* and *rasa*.
But that which consists of *haṃsapadā* is [so called] because of the letters *repha* (*ra*) and *śa*.
These five *svarabhaktis* are to be avoided when they are not to be pronounced; they are to be excluded from the sequence.

(30) Where a *svarabhakti* arises with a vowel, it consists of one syllable (*ekapadā*); where it is seen to arise with a consonant, it is traditionally remembered as consisting of two syllables (*dvipadā*). (31)
A consonant should have a duration of one-quarter mātrā, and likewise a vowel should have one-and-a-half mātrās; this is designated as *svarabhakti*.
A wise person, when pronouncing the *svarabhaktis*, should avoid three faults.
By abandoning the defects of being swallowed, one should likewise [perceive] the vowel *i* and the vowel *u*;
for just as the white moonstone, when overcome by the luster of sapphire during the new and full moon, indeed assumes a blue state.
In the same way, the entire vowel, when overwhelmed by the qualities of the nasal [anusvāra], attains the status of a subordinate element (aṅga).
The vowel *raṅga* is produced from the heart and emerges like [the sound of] bell-metal;
it is both short and of two morae (*dvimātra*), as illustrated by the example "dadatva. 34–35.

The noble person should apply the vowel *u* before the consonant *ha*; when followed by *ś*, *ṣ*, or *sa*, it is produced with a vowel. That which is opened wide by *ś*, *ṣ*, or *sa* is known as the *hari-sannata* (the lion’s roar). 36.
When the two rays are joined, the fault is like that of a hundred-year-old calf; this is the illustration.
Its measure, however, is the size of an atom in the heart, but in the head it is the size of an atom; O Aṅga, the practice of these atoms at the tip of the nose has been fully proclaimed.
The *raṅga* does not exist without the vowel *svara*, nor likewise without the letter *ṅa*.
Through the conjunction of both, it is designated as *raṅga*.
When followed by *r*, they call it *raṅgam*; in the case of unvoiced consonants, it is produced through the mouth and nose. 38–39.

But when followed by a vowel, the nasal [anusvāra] occurs, while the *stanamadhya* (the middle of the chest) is employed for the two [sounds] *ṛ* and *ṝ*, as in *ṛtūṃ* and *ṛtuyate*; *bhrātṛvyavau* and *strannate* are examples; *gomān* is [an example of] *agre* (at the beginning).
The disappearance of a sound is elision (*lopa*), while the appearance of a sound is augmentation (*āgama*).
A change in color (varṇa) constitutes a modification (vikāra), while the inherent nature (svabhāva) is known as the original form (prakṛti).

Among those words, conjunction (sandhi) is declared to be fourfold; however, it is certain that elision (lopa), augmentation (āgama), and modification (vikāra) constitute the original form (prakṛti). 41–42.
The elision-sandhi (lopasaṃdhi) is exemplified by *salokasaś-candre*; the augment (*āgama*) is remembered as in *vājisi-iti*.
Furthermore, the modification (*vikāra*) is seen in *vāji*, while the original form (*prakṛti*) is *kaścit*.
One should know that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs in *tṛṇavat*, and the substitution of *ṣ* occurs in *suṣupuṣi*.
The wise one causes the long ritual procedure for the prosperity of the sacrifice to fall away;
when the grass has been well-spread, they perform the omission of the action, resulting in the loss of the syllable when the food is lost.
One should know that in the *Cārāyaṇīyaka*, there is elision (*dralopa*) due to these six [conditions]:

in a single word (*ekapada*), in the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), likewise in what arises from the pause between words (*padāvagraha*), when making a hiatus in the place [of the pause], and in the three steps (*tri-prakrama-pada*). (45–46)
He who conquers that village without ever approaching it—Kāṭaka, Samagra, Himavat, and Keśava; these four are immeasurable according to the Śruti by virtue of their qualities within the cave. 47.
The perception of phonemes (varṇa-saṃjñā), conjunction (saṃyoga), as well as the formation of euphonic combination (saṃhitā-karaṇa),

the measure of morae (mātrā-pramāṇa), the hand (hasta), vowels (svara), tremors (kampa), transitions (vivṛtti), the vowel-portions (svarabhakti), the movement of the foot (pādavṛtta), and the modes of recitation (vṛtti) regarding that which is consumed and that which is not consumed. 48.
This sequence has been explained as previously stated; now follows the definition of the sequence.
Thus ends the eighth chapter.
Having formed the *saṃhitā* of two words, one should pause between each word and word.
Having first set aside the [first] conjunction, one should join each subsequent word with the following one;
for you, O Asita,
those three steps have their terminuses such that your stride consists of three steps.
Having first released [the previous one], the wise man should proceed once again;
he should join the deity [with the new one], and the four-step procedure should be performed in the same manner as the three-step rite.
One should first step back foot by foot and then advance again;
[these are] the words ending in vowels for the gods, beginning with *du*, *dā*, etc., as prescribed by the rules of vowel sandhi.
These two produce the triple sequence of both the *u* and the *ṇa*;
they have approached with the sacred word (*brahman*), lifting up the truth (*ṛta*) from its beginning, moving forward according to their will. May he, being well-disposed, [grant] prosperity.

The letter *u* should be placed between the two feet, followed by a non-conjunct (*apṛkta*) vowel; this is to be known as the "threefold transgression" (*trikrama*) along with the third [syllable]. Likewise, one should indicate the letter *ā*.
Wherever the verse *ud u tyam* occurs, the two causes—the transgression and the agent—should come together.
Between any two words, there is a fourfold sequence of four;
this is the case for the word *punar* in the phrase *punaraimi*, where the vowel *a* in *pragrahyāṇām* serves as the illustration.
However, this does not apply at the end of a sequence, nor with respect to a *sahitā* (euphonic combination).

The *urvī*, the two *rodasī*, the *ṛc*s, the *ardharca*s, the *anuvāka*s, as well as that which consists of a single word (*ekapada*), when unjoined and not to be joined together, is known as the *saṃhāra*;
it is observed by the sages who are free from birth and death.

The preceding word is unaccented (anudātta), while the subsequent word is high-pitched (udātta). In the *prakrama*, one should prescribe the high pitch for those words that are being joined together. For all [varieties] beginning with the *jāti*, a transverse step (*tiryak-prakramaṇa*) is prescribed.
One should indicate that these [syllables] have no predecessor as being *udātta*;
the word would become *svarita* due to the subsequent *phala* sounds. The wise one should step forward straight with the feet.
"In the highest heaven, the two wives ascended. (RV 10.85.40)
One should indicate the sequence there by means of the third [vowel], beginning with the vowels, starting from "sa" and ending with "apūrva" and "it".
And those two [syllables] should likewise be situated after the upadeśa.
One should assign that fourfold sequence according to the aforementioned *sandhi*:
first, the two-footed [verse] belongs to Aṅgiras; then the three-footed belongs to the Vālakhilyas; and the four-footed belongs to Māṣakumbhī. 14–15.

Regarding the repetition of words previously mentioned, there shall indeed be an avoidance [of fault] once the wise one has performed the junction of the commencement and then brought it to a conclusion with "devāvāstosvāha."
But elsewhere, when there is another word intended as a repetition, one should form two or three words [together] according to the characteristics of the stated sequence;
"May Savitṛ raise it up."
The characteristics prescribed in the scriptures for the *prakramas* have been stated in due order;
hereafter, however, those pertaining specifically to the junctions (*saṃdhi*) of the *veṣṭakas* are described.
These consist of fourfold [rules]: the substitution of *ṣatva*, *ṇatva*, elision (*upāra*), and lengthening (*dīrghatva*).
In whatever word it may cease, that is characterized as *samāyāta*.
Chapter Nine:
[The topics are] non-attachment to the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) and the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) from the process of manifestation (*vivarta*).
*Ādara*, *parihāra*, and *śabda* are synonymous terms.

According to the scriptures, those [notes] which are subject to *parihāra*— namely the *avagraha*, the *samāpādya*, the *pragrahya*, and the *naidhanas*— are to be repeated after being joined together.

One should know the rule for the *parihāra* [recitation] as "suṣupuṣī urvī" (2). Having formed the *saṃhitā* up to the end with "vidhiṃ vidyāt saṃyojya abhyasyate punaḥ," one should begin again as if reciting in *pada* form. (3)
In cases where the word *prapra* occurs—
whether it ends in the vowel *ā* or is long or protracted— the *eṣaṇdhi* (vowel coalescence) must always be applied there in the *parihāra* (avoidance) formulas. 4.
In the case of euphonic combinations (*sandhi-varṇa*) where *śe* remains, there shall be a hiatus (*vivṛtti*) before a following vowel;
for a word ending in *u*, it becomes *va* before an *i*-vowel, and one should prescribe the change to *ī*. 5.
In the words *aṃhomuce*, *anumatyai*, and *aṣṭākapālaḥ*, one should not elide the *t* when it follows the vowel *a*; however, upon its transformation (*vivartana*), one should insert the letter *r*.
For these [words] always begin with a guttural (*kaṇṭhya*) vowel followed by *r*.
"Mayo bhūḥ vātaḥ vena āvaḥ";
for when these [mantras] are recited, one should indeed become "bhuvaḥ," the single name to be known, devoid of the letter *r*.
All other instances of the word "bhuvaḥ" must be carefully made to include the *repha* (the letter *r*). 7.
You have become one who possesses the cosmic order (*ṛtāvān*) and is worthy of sacrifice; yet again, you are proclaimed as the one who shines forth.
You are the light of heaven, the light of the day, the light of every day, the illuminator of the night, the protector of the earth, and likewise the one who is bowed down in prayer.
The Udgātṛ, the Prātar-unnetṛ, the Hotṛ, and likewise the Neṣṭṛ;
the Dvāravibha-raja-āga and the Dvārabhāḥ-sannata—these are the specific steps that have arisen separately from him. 9–10.
In the *Cārāyaṇīyaka*, those [words] following a *repha* should always be avoided;
having established the *avagraha*, there are the *pragṛhya* vowels and the *naiyana*s. There is respect for words and phonemes, except for the *durohaṇa* and *akait*.

In the word *aśvavantam*, there is the *vardhanata* [defect]; likewise in *dūrohaṇam*. However, if the two sounds *ṣ* and *t* occur in a single word separated by a guttural (*kaṇṭhya*), one should not consider that as a fault. 12–13.

They cast the *śukta* (sour gruel), iron is brought forward; there is the elision of the *repha* when [the word] *svapantau* occurs. There should be *upadhā* in the sense of "acceptance. One should indicate the horse with the heavy *sakāra* in the phrase *svarṣāyantu*.

Except for the *dūrohaṇa* chant, after this point [the verses] are concluded; the two *naidhana* refrains should be understood according to their respective positions. Where the first word is *dundubhaḥ*, it attains the status of the third word in the *parigraha*.
The wise say that the fifth [vowels] are unchanging;
however, for all the vowels beginning with *svara*, there is a transformation (*vivartana*) into the letter *ya* when following a sacrificial formula (*yajña*). 17.

One should not indicate a short or long vowel as being homogeneous with the letter *i*; [the rules for] *ṛ* and *ṝ* apply here to *i* and *ī*. A wise man should cause all conjunct consonants followed by the particle *iti* to undergo elision.
Those [syllables] ending in *i* that are not joined with *i* do not undergo elision (*chavarjitāḥ*) when followed by *kāra*. 19.
Those [syllables] ending in *ā* that are followed by *svasām* [become] like *chā* before *mokṣa*; at the end of an *anuvāka*, however, there is *sāraṇā* at the end of a *prakrama*. 20.

If those two [planets] are situated in debilitation, one should likewise predict that the person will meet an ignoble end; moreover, at the time of reciting the words, one should always indicate that very liberation which corresponds to whichever syllable is abandoned when a planet is situated in its debilitation sign.
Thus, the word *iti* is the word for liberation; the word for grasping begins with a vowel.
Having placed the final syllable in front, one should indicate it upon the preceding syllable.
When the word being struck is in a low (deficient) state, it is destroyed in its prior member. 22–23.
If it is preceded by a low (nīca) tone, it shall be like a word; if preceded by a high (ucca) tone, it shall be low.

At the end of a *svarita* [syllable], for the purpose of release (*vimokṣa*), there is liberation from the remaining phonemes. In connection with another member of a compound, it is struck down (emphasized) just like a word.

If, at the end of the release, a pair of syllables remains situated upon the support, one should know that to be the "grasping" (grahaṇa), and the "releasing" (mokṣaṇa) would have occurred prior to it;
if a flowing forth (syandana) is observed during the junction of the releasing and the grasping. 25–26.
One should perform *syandana* (gliding) and *sāraṇa* (flowing); before that, there should be *mokṣaṇa* (release).

From a *svarita* vowel, there is *grahaṇa* (seizing), and from the remainder of the foot, there is *vimokṣaṇa* (liberation). Like a word (*pada*), it may be preceded by a *nīca* (grave) vowel; it should be *nīca* when preceded by an *uchcha* (acute) vowel.

At the end of *mokṣa*, there is a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel; the word beginning with *su* is the term for "seizing" (*grahaṇa*). Alternatively, whether situated in the high (*udātta*) or low (*nīca*) tone, liberation (*vimokṣaṇa*) occurs from the remainder of the phonemes.
A word ending in *e* is "liberation" (*mokṣa*), while the word beginning with a vowel is "seizing" (*grahaṇa*).
One should perform the release at the letter *e*, and likewise the grasping at the letter *a*.
For one who has released the earth, liberation comes from the letter *a*; it is the supreme state.
When [the breath] is released, one should perform the release; one should avoid a phoneme that leaves a phoneme as a remainder.

Upon release, one should go to the *u* vowel; in the first case, it goes to the following syllable, while in the other case, it goes to the subsequent syllable. One should always cause the second syllable to be grasped at the time of release.
However, if a circumflex (*svarita*) is observed at the end of a repetition, [the rule is as follows].
If there is a low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), the release (*mokṣaṇa*) should occur on a high-pitched vowel (*udātta*);

for all vowels beginning with those that are high-pitched at the end, there should be a recollection of their respective phonetic characteristics. One should likewise indicate the first vowel as high-pitched twice, and the second as well.
One who is a celibate student, one who conducts himself well, one who is intelligent, and likewise one who performs his duties;
one who is dear, one who bestows wealth, and one who imparts knowledge;
one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one who is obedient, one who possesses faith, and likewise one who asks questions—[these are those from whom one should learn]. (34–35)

The fruit that one enjoys by giving away the entire earth filled with wealth three times to Brahmins— provided those twice-born ones are devoted to the study of the Vedas and are endowed with self-restraint and tranquility—
that same fruit belongs to one who practices meditation on the Supreme beyond darkness.
Some proceed by means of Sāṃkhya, and some, being practitioners of yoga, proceed by means of Yoga;
yet only certain great-souled ones proceed by the study of the Krama— namely,
those who are knowers of all scriptures and those people who are knowers of the Krama.
Having attained the state of a single meaning, they indeed enter Hari;
fifty-six [verses] are in the first [chapter], thirty in the second,
thirty-two are stated in the third, and twenty-nine in the fourth.
In the fifth [chapter], thirty-six are proclaimed; indeed, forty-seven in the sixth.
Forty verses are indeed celebrated in the eighth, while thirteen are in the ninth;
forty verses are indeed fully described in the tenth. 40–41.
This treatise of Ārāyaṇīya is renowned as consisting of exactly three hundred and forty verses;
it should be given to one who is free from envy, but never to one who is envious.
But what is given to one who is envious is like seed sown in barren soil.
He who recites this constantly, he who causes a twice-born man to study it,
and he who truly understands its meaning, goes to the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the Ārāyaṇīya-Śikṣā.
